questions.question: Why does load_safetensors need a pretrained-to-local name map?
options: Published GPT-2 keys such as wte and h.0.attn.c_attn must be translated to local names such as tok_embed and blocks.0.attn.qkv.
The map decrypts the safetensors payload before PyTorch can read it.
The map changes the model vocabulary to match the checkpoint automatically.
The map chooses a random seed for each transformer block.
questions.explanation: make_pretrained_to_local is a literal mapping between the checkpoint naming convention and the parameter names returned by the local model.

questions.question: Which published GPT-2 weights does _needs_transpose identify before assignment?
options: Only wte.weight and wpe.weight, because embeddings are the only two-dimensional tensors.
The Conv1D-layout projection weights ending in c_attn.weight, c_proj.weight, or c_fc.weight; they are transposed for nn.Linear.weight.
Every bias and LayerNorm tensor, because one-dimensional tensors need a transpose too.
Only the final ln_f tensors, because the local model stores LayerNorm backwards.
questions.explanation: The checkpoint uses the TensorFlow-style Conv1D layout for attention and MLP projections. The loader transposes those matrices, but leaves embeddings, biases, and LayerNorm vectors alone.

questions.question: After wte.weight is loaded, how does the loader reconstruct the tied language-model head?
options: It reads lm_head.weight from a second safetensors file.
It computes the head from the last hidden state without storing parameters.
It aliases model.lm_head.weight to model.tok_embed.weight, so both names share storage.
It copies the position embedding into the head because both have two dimensions.
questions.explanation: The checkpoint omits a separate LM-head tensor. With weight tying enabled, assigning the token embedding and then aliasing the head recreates the shared parameter.

questions.question: What does load_safetensors do when a mapped tensor has the wrong shape?
options: It truncates the checkpoint tensor to fit the local parameter.
It assigns the tensor and records a warning for a later audit.
It pads the tensor with zeros until the local shape matches.
It records the pair in LoadReport.shape_mismatch and skips assignment, leaving the local parameter unchanged.
questions.explanation: The loader checks shapes before adding an assignment to its pending list. A mismatch is reported and no partial copy is performed.

questions.question: Why does make_stub_safetensors use GPT-2-style names and shapes instead of a real download?
options: It keeps the demo offline and small while exercising the same name-map, transpose, shape-check, and weight-tying path as a real file.
Real GPT-2 checkpoints cannot be represented in safetensors.
A stub avoids constructing the local model, so the loader can be tested without parameters.
The loader only accepts files whose tensors were generated with seed 42.
questions.explanation: The fixture is synthetic in values but faithful in key names and tensor shapes for the configured small model. Replacing it with a compatible real checkpoint does not change the loader logic.

questions.question: What evidence does the demo collect before and after loading the fixture?
options: It compares only wall-clock time, so a faster forward pass proves every tensor landed.
It records a parameter fingerprint and a deterministic sample; a changed fingerprint/sample is a sanity signal that the load affected the model, while LoadReport supplies coverage details.
It changes the tokenizer vocabulary and checks whether decoding becomes shorter.
It resets the random seed after loading and treats any new seed as proof of successful mapping.
questions.explanation: _state_fingerprint and quick_generate provide a coarse before/after signal. They complement, rather than replace, the report's loaded, missing, unexpected, and mismatch lists.
